entries.title: S. Korea warns of AI-aided hacking after bank data breaches
entries.summary: Seoul is alarmed after a recent breach of South Korean banks' cyber defenses that reportedly involved AI-assisted hacking. Officials warn such methods could be used to also target other sectors and government agencies.
entries.content:
South Korea

S. Korea warns of AI-aided hacking after bank data breaches

October 8, 2026

Seoul is alarmed after a recent breach of South Korean banks' cyber defenses that reportedly involved AI-assisted hacking. Officials warn such methods could be used to also target other sectors and government agencies.

The South Korean government has demanded a comprehensive overhaul of safeguards against hackers after seven of the nation's major financial institutions' cyber defenses were breached last week and the private data of thousands of customers was leaked. 

The data breaches go beyond the financial sector, with two of the largest churches in the country and Korea Electric Power Corp. on Wednesday confirming that their online systems had been illegally accessed, although it is not clear whether the same perpetrator was responsible for all the attacks.

On Tuesday, Prime Minister Han Seong-sook called for measures to be taken swiftly to halt any further leaks.

"This is a serious situation because this incident is believed to have taken advantage of artificial intelligence, and if AI is used in phishing attacks, it could lead to secondary damage," Yonhap News quoted Han as saying at a Cabinet meeting.

"It is also a serious situation in that similar hacking methods could spread beyond the financial sector to industries, as well as government and public sectors."

Threats to other sectors

Han said government agencies, public institutions, the financial sector and private enterprises all need to "remain vigilant."

Early reports from the US-based cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike suggest that the attack may have originated in China, although South Korea's Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) said it had identified 28 internet protocol addresses in the United States, Japan, Germany and at least 10 other countries that were involved in the bank breaches.

"South Korea officials are being careful about how they are framing their findings," said Aditya Das, an analyst at cryptocurrency research firm Brave New Coin in Auckland, New Zealand.

In the bank logs, investigators found traces of a tool called ARTEX, an open-source "autonomous penetration-testing" agent built by a Chinese developer, he said.

"It is freely available on the internet and officials have said explicitly that a Chinese-built tool doesn't mean Chinese attackers," Das told DW, adding that the use of multiple IP addresses is likely to be "a ploy by the hackers to hide their tracks."

It appears that the hackers exploited weak authentication protocols in portals used by external loan recruiters, employees' mobile tools and sales-support systems.

Data on thousands of customers lost

According to South Korean media reports, data belonging to as many as 68,000 customers was taken, with Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and Hana Bank among the worst affected. Names, phone numbers, annual income figures, loan limits and their loan products were accessed, along with a small number of national identification numbers.

Das pointed out that if a scammer has a person's name, phone number, income figure and is aware that the individual has recently applied for a loan, a fake "bank security" call can be very convincing to the unwary. Once a victim has transferred funds to an account specified by the scammer, it is very difficult to get it back.

Hyobin Lee, a professor at Sogang University in Seoul, says the seriousness of the incident goes far beyond the simple exposure of personal information.

"If criminals obtain such information, they may be able to carry out sophisticated financial fraud, identity theft, or highly targeted phishing attacks," she said.

"Another concern is that stolen personal information can be reused or combined with other leaked databases, potentially creating security risks that persist long after the original attack," Lee underlined.

"More broadly, such incidents can undermine public confidence in financial institutions and raise concerns about the security of the financial system as a whole."

While major financial institutions have invested heavily in protecting their core systems, such as internet banking and mobile banking platforms, Lee said they have overlooked other elements of their networks.

"Some auxiliary systems, such as loan agent information portals and internal mobile applications used by employees, appear to have received less security attention," she said, adding that the application of AI by the hackers is another concerning element.

AI makes hacking easier?

"In the past, identifying security vulnerabilities, developing malicious code and conducting attacks against financial institutions required substantial technical expertise and considerable time," Lee pointed out. "Today, generative AI tools can assist with writing computer code, analyzing software vulnerabilities, processing large amounts of information and automating certain stages of cyber operations."

AI is "lowering the technical barriers to cybercrime" and making it accessible to more bad actors. At the same time, the technology is ramping up the speed and scale of attacks to overwhelm cyber defenses.

Given those developments, Lee fears that AI-assisted cyberattacks are only going to become more frequent.

"And the risks will not be limited to financial institutions," she said. "Hospitals, government agencies, energy infrastructure, telecommunications networks and other organizations holding sensitive information may also become increasingly attractive targets."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: India news: Opposition doubles down against poll chief after detentions
entries.summary: India's opposition alliance is gearing up for another day of protests after demonstrating lawmakers were detained for the second time. Meanwhile, India is seeking to repatriate its nationals working in Russian military.
entries.content:
India

India news: Opposition doubles down after detentions

Published October 8, 2026last updated October 8, 2026

India's opposition alliance is gearing up for another day of protests after demonstrating lawmakers were detained for the second time. Meanwhile, India is seeking to repatriate its nationals working in Russian military.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • India's opposition alliance set to stage another protest against the chief election commissioner in Delhi
  • India's Cockroach group to stage similar protest in Bengaluru
  • Cockroach party claims 1000s of volunteers detained across states ahead of Delhi march
  • Foreign Ministry seeks update from Moscow about remaining Indian nationals working for Russian military
  • Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker detained in US
  • Indian workers who built US consulate in Milan agree to record payout

Here are the top headlines from India on Thursday, October 8:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed. 

Skip next section CJP's Dipke vows to 'hit the streets' till election chief resigns

CJP's Dipke vows to 'hit the streets' till election chief resigns

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke said he, along with other demonstrators, would continue to protest until Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigned, while speaking at a protest in the southern city of Bengaluru over the mass deletion of voters from India's electoral rolls.

"One two three four, Narendra Modi vote thief," the crowd chanted on Dipke's direction. The slogan rhymes when spoken in Hindi.

Other slogans at the event included calls for dismissing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. That's the exercise that led to the deletion of over 130 million Indian voters from record in the first place. Dipke also accused Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi of "murdering democracy."

Today's demonstrations in Bengaluru will include a 'People's Tribunal,' Indian media reported, where people from across the southern state are expected to attend and outline their grievances with SIR. That will be followed by a march.

If you're looking for the details on what the protest is about, why opposition leaders and activists are calling for the election chief's resignation and how this relates to PM Modi, scroll a few posts below to our brief explainer.

Skip next section Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker detained in US

Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker detained in US

A filmmaker whose award-winning work has explored conflict in his native Kashmir has been detained by United States immigration officials on suspicion of residing and working in the country illegally.

Arfat Sheikh was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after disembarking a flight from California at Washington Dulles International Airport on September 24, according to a statement from friends and relatives who labeled his detention "unlawful" and are calling for his release.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, confirmed to the Reuters news agency on Wednesday that Sheikh had "legally entered the US on a temporary basis and illegally overstayed his lawful admittance."

Sheikh, 42, entered the US in 2019 on a student visa and enrolled on a graduate course in film studies at Georgia State University, according to the statement from friends and family.

Having applied for asylum in 2020, the statement said he had a ​pending immigration application and was authorized to work and live in the US. It did not mention the ground for asylum.

Sheikh, who hails from India-administered Kashmir, won the Emerging Filmmaker Activist Award at the Teaneck International Film Festival in 2025.

Skip next section EXPLAINER — Global power shifts: How Europe is turning to India

EXPLAINER — Global power shifts: How Europe is turning to India

India and Europe are moving closer. Trade is one driver, but strategy matters more. As US reliability is questioned and China’s rise reshapes geopolitics, can they build a lasting partnership?

Wacth the full video:

Skip next section Opposition creating 'atmosphere of anarchy,' says Modi's party

Opposition creating 'atmosphere of anarchy,' says Modi's party

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party on Thursday slammed protesting opposition leaders for "creating an atmosphere of anarchy" and "undermining the constitution," according to Press Trust of India.

This comes as hundreds of opposition lawmakers including Modi's arguably biggest challenger, Rahul Gandhi, protests in New Delhi over 'vote theft' and demands the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.

"It would not be wrong to say that all the allegations being levelled by Rahul Gandhi, Arvind Kejriwal and various Opposition parties, that democracy is being destroyed, raise the question: what is the basis for these allegations?" BJP National Spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said at a press conference in Delhi.

"These are baseless allegations being leveled by an irresponsible opposition. The claim that democracy is being destroyed and that the constitution is being undermined has no basis and not an iota of evidence," he told reporters.

Protests, but after lunch

Indian opposition leaders are scheduled to protest in central Delhi today for the third straight day, without police permission. As per Indian media, Indian National Congress (INC) President Mallikarjun Kharge is hosting protesting MPs at a well-known eatery not far from the designated protest site of Jantar Mantar. They will likely protest after lunch.

On Wednesday, the lawmakers met at a different eatery followed by a march towards the Election Commission of India (ECI).

Skip next section Veteran actor Nana Patekar dies at 75

Veteran actor Nana Patekar dies at 75

Nana Patekar, a well-known Indian actor and filmmaker, died on Thursday after what Indian media reported was a severe heart attack. He was 75.

Patekar passed away at his home in the scenic state of Goa but was later taken to a hospital where doctors pronounced him dead, news agency Press Trust of India reported.

It said Patekar was found unconscious in his apartment and could not be revived despite 45 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Authorities will conduct postmortem procedures to ascertain the cause of the death, the report said.

Patekar's film career

Born in 1951 in the western state of Maharashtra, Patekar built his career over five decades, largely in Hindi and Marathi-language cinema. He was known for his intense, often complex roles, punctuated with unconventional comedy.

In his early work, he earned acclaim for movies like "Parinda" where he played a ruthless crime lord in the menacing setting of the underworld-dominant Mumbai. One of his better-loved movies includes "Khamoshi" — a musical in which Patekar portrays Joseph, a loving yet stubborn deaf and mute father to the lead actress.

India's millennials saw the actor in lighter, comedy dramas like "Taxi No. 9211" where he played a taxi driver who wrecks havoc in a rich man's life after accidentally coming in possession of the key to the latter's wealth. Still, one of his most memorable roles will be that of underworld boss Uday Shetty in the 2007 movie "Welcome." His iconic dialogue from the movie are often meme-d and casually repeated among groups of friends.

Patekar was the recipient of three National Film Awards, several Indian Cinema Awards and state awards. He also received a Padma Shree, India's fourth-highest civilian honor.

#MeToo allegations

In 2018, during India's #MeToo movement, an actress accused Patekar of sexually harassing her on the sets of a movie in 2008.

The actress alleged that he was present on the sets of song which did not feature him and tried to physically get close to her under the pretext of teaching dance moves.

Authorities had launched a formal investigation into the claims, which Patekar consistently denied. The probe was closed approximately a year later due to the lack of sufficient evidence.

Skip next section India denies bias after Musk's 'oligarchs' jab, says satellite rules 'fair'

India denies bias after Musk's 'oligarchs' jab, says satellite rules 'fair'

India on Thursday defended its satellite internet approval process, hours after US tech mogul Elon Musk accused unnamed "oligarchs" of blocking Starlink's launch in the country. 

In a post on X, Musk had said "certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people," were blocking Starlink from entering the Indian market.

"You can guess who they are... This is a crime against the people of India!" he added.

India's telecom market is currently dominated by billionaires Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Jio and Sunil Mittal's Airtel. Both their satellite internet ventures, along with Musk's Starlink, have secured early approvals in India but are awaiting spectrum assignments.

For Starlink, this wait has stretched on for four years.

"The suggestion that the ‌framework ​or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived," officials said in a statement. "Security assessment as part of this process is currently under way in respect of all the three licensees. As and when this process is completed for a licensed entity, it may proceed to the next step," the statement read.

Musk has previously too been at odds with Mittal and Ambani over how India should assign spectrum reach.

FYI: spectrum refers to the invisible radio frequencies which enable mobile calls, text messages, and data transmission.

For Musk's Starlink, at stake is access to a satellite broadband market which Deloitte forecasts will be worth $1.9 billion by 2030.

Starlink's India saga also features a layer of India-US diplomacy. Washington has pushed for greater access for Starlink as a goodwill marker in trade talks with countries burdened with President Donald Trump's tariffs. All of this while New Delhi and Washington are yet to finalize a trade deal since reaching an interim framework in February.

Skip next section Indian workers who built US consulate in Milan agree to record payout

Indian workers who built US consulate in Milan agree to record payout

Foreign workers, mostly Indian, building a vast new US consulate compound in Milan, Italy, signed agreements on Wednesday securing payouts averaging tens of thousands of euros each.

The payout is over alleged labor abuses while working for an American construction company.

Over 60 laborers signed the deal to receive their share of a €31 million (nearly $35 million) settlement with Alabama-based Caddell Construction. Prosecutors say this is the largest-ever settlement over labor exploitation in Europe.

The payouts include unpaid overtime, reimbursement for housing illegally deducted from their pay and other hefty damages sought by the prosecutors.

Dilip Ram, a 43-year-old mason from India who worked at the Milan site for over two years, said that the money would go a long way to help his family of five in the Indian state of Bihar.

"Things are better now than before …we get more rest now," Ram said, after signing the deal. "This has led to a lot of change. This settlement will be good. Because the workers had troubles, that’s why this settlement has been applied."

Prosecutors alleged that workers were paid less than $2 (€1.8) an hour, were illegally docked money for housing and denied overtime for working up to 10 hours a day, six days a week. They were reportedly also subjected to threats and not given proper medical care when injured on the job.

While most of the workers were from India, others were from Nigeria, Kenya and Bangladesh.

The Indian workers reported having to pay €5,000 ($5,600) to recruiters to get the jobs. However, the current settlement could not address abuses in India as that is out of its jurisdiction.

Skip next section India seeks update from Moscow on Indian nationals working with Russian military

India seeks update from Moscow on Indian nationals working with Russian military

India has sought an update from Russian authorities on the whereabouts of 69 Indian nationals reportedly working for the Russian military, Indian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told reporters on Wednesday evening.

Jaiswal said this during a routine media briefing. The ministry has been consistently urging Moscow to repatriate all Indian nationals serving in the Russian military since it found outthat some 259 people had been recruited into the armed forces since the war in Ukraine began. 

"Of these, through our efforts, so far, 139 Indian nationals have seen early discharge from the Russian Army," Jaiswal said.

"We are following up with the Russian authorities for updates on the whereabouts of 69 Indian nationals who are reportedly with the Russian Army," he added.

51 Indians have died so far while fighting for Russia on the front lines of Ukraine, according to Indian media.

Jaiswal warned against the "grave danger" of taking up jobs in the Russian military, saying "I once again want to urge that Indian nationals must stay away from offers being made to join the Russian Army."

Skip next section Cockroach party claims 1000s of volunteers detained across states ahead of Delhi march

Cockroach party claims 1000s of volunteers detained across states ahead of Delhi march

While India's opposition is protesting against the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC), so are other activists and student groups.

One such group is pressure group the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) which has already led a protest demanding CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation in western city of Mumbai, earlier this week. They are scheduled to participate in a similar protest in Bengaluru today and lead one in Delhi on October 10.

CJP co-convener Ashutosh Ranka on Thursday claimed that thousands of the group's volunteers had been detained across states like Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal "on the grounds that they were planning to attend the October 10th protest."

"How many will you arrest? There are over 250 million cockroaches," he said on X, using the group's chosen term for its supporters.

"Modi thinks he can silence dissent by putting people behind bars. The more people you detain, the more people will show up!" CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke said in a post on X.

Police authorities in these states have not commented on the matter so far.

Skip next section All you need to know about the protests

All you need to know about the protests

What prompted the protests?

Pressure on Kumar intensified in September after the Indian Express newspaper reported that two of the three election commissioners had formally raised concerns over aspects of the Special Intensive Revisions (SIR) at least 14 times over the past 10 months.

The objections relate to new voter registrations, deletion and restoration of voters in the rolls, filing of appeals against orders restoring voters in the SIR process and the custody and security of the entire electoral roll itself, the report said.

In one of the objections, Commissioner Sukhbir Singh Sandhu reportedly complained that the Kumar acted against the written advice of himself and Commissioner Vivek Joshi and claimed his actions was "unauthorized and illegal."

However, the Election Commission of India (ECI) issued a statement dismissing concerns of an internal rift, saying differing views were a "normal" part of deliberations and that all its actions were lawful.

How many people were excluded?

According to Election Commission data cited by Indian media, over 130 million names have been excluded from the draft electoral rolls since the revision began in October 25. That's roughly the population of Mexico. In India, it adds up to about 15% of the electorate.

Not all the exclusions are contested as they also took double entries and deaths into account.

A clearer idea of wrongfully excluded voters can only emerge after the exercise is complete across the nation.

How has the election body responded?

After denying a rift, the ECI has since taken a number of measures to improve internal procedures and transparency. It has also directed a "special drive" in 20 states and union territories to include voters who have been left out of the rolls due to solvable errors.

How do these protests relate to Modi and his party?

The protests against CEC Gyanesh Kumar are partially being viewed as renewed pressure on Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

The reason behind it may not be immediately obvious since the ECI is meant to be an independent body. But this might help:

The commission is responsible for overseeing elections and related projects such as the SIR exercise, which is meant to remove redundancies in India's electoral rolls.

Opposition leaders and critics have argued that those struck off in the exercise include a heavy proportion of minority voters and that Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP is using it as a tool to secure future electoral wins. They have also accused ECI chief Kumar of doing the central government's bidding even though the institute is meant to maintain its independence.

The BJP has dismissed those claims, arguing that those removed largely involve dead voters and illegal infiltrators, thereby protecting India's democracy.

Skip next section India's opposition alliance plans third day of protest against election chief

India's opposition alliance plans third day of protest against election chief

A bloc of Indian political parties, in alliance against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP party, is expected to stage a protest in central Delhi on Thursday to demand the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged misconduct. 

Opposition leaders including Indian National Congress' Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Vadra are visibly at the forefront of the protest.

On Tuesday, Gandhi, Vadra, their supporters and over 200 allied Members of Parliament (MPs) marched on the Election Commission of India (ECI) to demand a meeting with Kumar. When blocked by the Delhi police, they began an impromptu sit in which ended with temporary detentions.

On Wednesday, the INC hosted a lunch-meeting in Delhi for about 200 MPs to discuss action against the CEC. Post lunch, they loaded up in buses to move towards the designated protest site of Jantar Mantar in central Delhi. Eventually on foot, the lawmakers were stopped by the police again.

A live feed on the YouTube channel of Gandhi's party showed police officials taking him into a vehicle and driving away. His sibling and lawmaker Vadra was also detained but taken to a different police station, as per Indian media.

Both were released sometime after 8:00 p.m local time (1430 GMT).

Gandhi and his fellow demonstrators have been demanding meetings with the Election Commission of India, Indian President Droupadi Murmu and a resignation from CEC Kumar.

They claim that Kumar is an agent of the Modi government and has been helping the Bharatiya Janata Party by rigging elections in their favor. These are significant and unprecedented accusations against the ECI — long regarded as one of the India's most trusted independent institutions.

"I am thankful to every INDIA alliance MP standing firm in defense of our democracy - in Parliament, outside on the streets, and today near Jantar Mantar. They can stop a march. They can refuse a meeting. But they cannot stop the will of our people," Gandhi said on a post on X. "Narendra Modi, Amit Shah, Gyanesh Kumar and the entire system will be brought to justice," he wrote.

Modi's party and the election body reject the allegations.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage!

Welcome to our coverage!

Good morning! And welcome to DW's India blog.

This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from Studio Delhi, and I will be your guide through the chaos of the Indian news cycle.

Protests against India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC), Gyanesh Kumar, over allegations of misconduct and bias, remain at the forefront with opposition leaders planning to stage protests in central Delhi for the third straight day. That's after opposition leader (and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's key competitor) Rahul Gandhi was detained by the police for a second time on Wednesday evening.

Gandhi seems to be aiming for a hat trick.

CEC Kumar is under fire for a controversial revision of electoral rolls in India which have reportedly deleted over 130 million voters from the official lists since the exercise began in 2025.

Aside from the opposition, the satirical Cockroach Janta Party said it will also peacefully demonstrate in the southern city of Bengaluru as it looks to mobilize all parts of the nation to "reclaim our democracy."

On the international front, India's Foreign Ministry said it has sought an update from Russian authorities on the whereabouts of some 69 Indian nationals. They are part of the group which was reportedly recruited for the Russian Army.

Stay tuned for all of this and more!

entries.title: Security in the Black Sea region: is Bulgaria the weak link in Europe's defense against threats from Russia?
entries.summary: Two ships have sunk off the coast of Bulgaria and Romania after drone attacks in recent days. Sofia has held back on pointing the finger at Russia. What does that mean for security in the Black Sea and the region?
entries.content:
Bulgaria

Security in the Black Sea region: Is Bulgaria a weak link?

October 8, 2026

Two ships have sunk off the coast of Bulgaria and Romania after drone attacks in recent days. Sofia has held back on pointing the finger at Russia. What does that mean for security in the Black Sea and the region?

Although security in the Baltic Sea and the threat of Russian provocation there are the subject of regular public debate, security in the Black Sea is a subject that sometimes gets less attention in the context of Russia's war in Ukraine even though the Black Sea is to a degree an active frontline in the war.

There are multiple reasons why the Black Sea's security is such a complex issue, but two incidents in recent days have highlighted just how precarious the situation there is.

On October 6, two cargo ships — the Alfa Watan and the Able — were struck by drones in the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.

The Alfa Watan sank, and its crew has not been recovered. Bulgaria conducted a search and rescue operation, which was called off on Wednesday morning.

The crew of the Able, which was damaged, was rescued by a passing Bulgarian ship. Two crew members were taken to the military hospital in Varna.

The day before, another cargo ship — the Royad Mammadov — was struck by a drone and sank off the coast of Romania. Two crew members lost their lives.

Multiple recent attacks on ships

These are not isolated incidents. In the past few months there have been multiple attacks on cargo ships carrying grain from Ukraine.

As a result, doubt is increasingly being cast on the belief that the western part of the Black Sea — the area off the coast of Bulgaria and Romania — is relatively safe.

"Тhe Black Sea front is clearly expanding, and we should no longer look only to the Baltic Sea as a potential avenue for escalation and aggressive actions," said Ruslan Trad, global security expert and non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council's Digital Forensic Research Lab.

PM downplays drone attacks

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev downplayed the attack on the ships, remarking that ships are constantly being sunk in the Black Sea and that Tuesday's drone attacks were "probably not the most serious incident."

Bulgaria's government called Tuesday's attack on the two vessels an "absolutely unacceptable violation of international law" but refrained from calling on Russia to end its war against Ukraine. 

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on the other hand, was unequivocal. He said that the Ukrainian military had assured Bulgaria that it was not responsible for the attack and pointed the finger squarely at Russia.

After a meeting of the National Security Council on Wednesday, a declaration was issued, which once again did not name the source of the threat in the Black Sea.

Radev stated that the cargo and the direction of travel of the ships "logically speaking" provide grounds for a hypothesis pointing to Russia but stressed that there is no concrete evidence. He also contradicted Zelenskyy, saying no such conversation had taken place.

Earlier he said that "if the war is not brought to an end in due time, it will continue to expand."

Similarly, Bulgaria's Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said that "we need to support all possible diplomatic efforts to bring this war to an end."

The refusal to state clearly that it is Russian aggression that is putting the region at risk is not new for the Radev administration.

Is Bulgaria a 'weak link' in European defense?

For Rumena Filipova, chairperson of the Institute of Global Analytics, this is an example of how Bulgaria seems to be a weak link in Europe's defense against malicious influence from Russia and China.

"This weakness stems from the lack of a serious institutional response to hybrid attacks of any kind, the absence of appropriate measures and a general tendency to downplay incidents," she told DW.

"The perpetrator is not named explicitly, even though our partners in the European Union and NATO have already issued numerous warnings about what aggressive steps Russia could take against Europe," she said.

According to Filipova, the Bulgarian government's narrative about peace without actually specifying the conditions or consequences for Ukrainian and European security is a demonstration of its leniency toward Moscow and raises the question of Sofia's geopolitical orientation.

No smoking gun

One of the surviving members of the Able's crew has said that he believes it was a Russian strike because the ship was carrying Ukrainian grain.

Ruslan Trad says that the crew member's testimony is an eyewitness hypothesis, not hard proof.

"The logic of motive, however, points toward Russia, as it is the state systematically threatening navigation to Ukrainian ports," he told DW, adding, "Until more concrete data is revealed the most accurate phrasing is 'probable but unproven Russian responsibility' without excluding other possibilities."

Trad also pointed out that Bulgarian institutions lack experience in attributing maritime drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone (EEZ). "When the system is uncertain, the safest institutional reaction is to say nothing until certainty is achieved," he said. "That is caution, but it is also a political choice."

Economic consequences

A direct military response or the triggering of NATO's Article 5, which guarantees collective defense in the event of an attack on any member state, should not be expected.

Bulgaria's EEZ in the Black Sea is not Bulgarian sovereign territory and, as such, the strikes on the ships in this zone do not constitute a direct attack on Bulgaria — or on Romania in the case of the Royad Mammadov.

Nevertheless, Ruslan Trad thinks these three incidents shatter the illusion that the western part of the Black Sea is a safe zone because of the distance between it and the frontlines in Ukraine.

"This will increase pressure for tighter maritime monitoring, anti‑mining capabilities, coordination between coastal guard services and intelligence‑sharing among allies," he said.

"The real effect will be a hardening of the shipping regime: stricter routing recommendations, higher insurance premiums and more difficulty hiring crews. Economic repercussions for local businesses can also be anticipated — imagine the impact on fishermen if they have to stay in ports constantly due to fear of further attacks. That is the intended effect of such strikes," he added.

Rumena Filipova believes that although Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey strengthened their Mine Countermeasures Black Sea Task Group at this year's NATO summit in Ankara, this is not enough.

She says there are far more substantial gaps in naval defense capabilities: "Modernization of Bulgaria's naval forces must be improved, much greater coordination — especially with Romania — is required. Yet, for more than a decade, Bulgarian authorities have downplayed or ignored the idea of developing joint naval defense forces and coordination, and that trend continues today," she said.

Turkey's leverage and China's role

Another question is how Turkey will react to recent developments. All three ships were owned by Turkish firms and some of the crew members were Turkish nationals. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Wednesday spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the security of navigation in the Black Sea.

Trad notes that Ankara has several levers of influence in the Black Sea: control of the Straits under the Montreux Convention, the largest fleet in the Black Sea and its role as a mediator between Moscow and Kyiv.

"A realistic scenario is intensified diplomacy, coordination with Bucharest and Sofia, and pressure for safe navigation, probably within the existing trilateral anti‑mining cooperation. If it turns out that Turkish citizens were killed in a deliberate attack, Ankara's stance could become markedly tougher," he said.

Filipova thinks that Black Sea security is already being perceived as a core issue — not only for the region but for NATO as a whole.

In her view, there's not enough coordination between the countries in the region, which means that any response to threats does not come from a united front — something she feels has to change urgently.

Filipova says that China's influence in the region and how it's connected with Russia is another factor.

"We see not only the concrete military threat from Russia but also a subtler threat from China, which is less publicly discussed. But Beijing is trying to acquire strategic assets in ports, thereby gaining influence over both trade and critical infrastructure," she said. "Given that China and Russia cooperate closely, this constitutes a double threat for the Black Sea region."

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

entries.title: French police arrest 5 suspects over Renoir museum theft
entries.summary: Thieves broke into the Renoir Museum on the French Riviera last month and made off with two paintings. The heist follows a string of high-profile robberies from European museums.
entries.content:
October 8, 2026

Thieves broke into the Renoir Museum on the French Riviera last month and made off with two paintings. The heist follows a string of high-profile robberies from European museums.

French police have arrested at least five suspects in connection with the theft of two Renoir paintings from a museum in southern France last month, local media reported.

Two burglars cut through a fence and smashed a window to enter the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on September 8. They then used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings, according to the local mayor.

The thieves initially took four Renoir artworks, valued together at around €9 million ($10.5 million), but dropped two in the museum's garden as they fled from police who had been alerted by the alarm system.

The daily Nice Martin newspaper, which first broke the news of the arrests, said six people were taken into custody, including the two suspected burglars.

Prosecutors in Marseille, who are leading the investigation, declined to comment.

What happened to the artworks?

The two paintings stolen from the museum were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).

Nice Martin reported that the whereabouts of the artworks was not immediately known.

Founded in 1960, the Renoir Museum is located in the former home and studio of French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir on the Cote d'Azur. The property houses 12 of his artworks and is surrounded by gardens and olive trees.

The heist in Cagnes-sur-Mer was the latest in a series of museum robberies, including the daylight theft of the French crown jewels from the Louvre Museum in Paris last year.

Four suspects have been arrested over that case, but the jewels they are accused of taking, with a value of around $100 million, have not been recovered.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: How a multibillion-dollar oilfield has ignited UK-Argentina feud over the Falklands
entries.summary: Argentina and the UK once fought a war over the Falkland Islands. Now the multibillion-dollar Sea Lion oil project has reignited old tensions, with Buenos Aires seeking to put a stop to the plans.
entries.content:
October 8, 2026

Argentina and the UK once fought a war over the Falkland Islands. Now the multibillion-dollar Sea Lion oil project has reignited old tensions, with Buenos Aires seeking to put a stop to the plans.

Home to less than 4,000 people and located in an isolated corner of the South Atlantic Ocean, the Falkland Islands don't often feature in global business headlines.

However, a UK-Israeli oil exploration project in its waters is stoking long-running tensions between Argentina and the people of the archipelago.

Argentina has laid claim to the islands for two centuries and refers to them as Las Malvinas. This 200-year-old dispute over the islands' sovereignty led to a 1982 war between the UK and Argentina, though British control was quickly restored after Argentine forces invaded the islands.

A 2013 sovereignty referendum on the islands returned a 99.8% vote in favor of remaining tied to the UK as a self-governing British Overseas Territory. Now the Sea Lion oilfield project has brought the issue back to the surface.

Last month, Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to launch an international legal challenge against the UK unless the project is stopped within two weeks.

The oil project is being operated by Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and the UK's Rockhopper Exploration and has the full support of the Falkand Islands Legislative Assembly, which has pursued the project since 2010. The companies plan to begin extracting oil from the Sea Lion oilfield by early 2028.

Milei says the project is "the illegal plundering of our resources" and that he will take the matter to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, an independent judicial body responsible for the application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.

Rally around the flag?

Stacy Bragger, a member of the Falklands Islands' 12-member assembly, told DW that the dispute was "nothing new" and that Argentina is using the oil project as "a vehicle to pursue their sovereignty claim."

He thinks Milei may be stepping up rhetoric ahead of the 2027 elections in Argentina.

"When there's elections coming up, the Falklands is a very convenient tool to use in order to rally people together and distract them from domestic problems," he said.

Henry Ziemer, an analyst with the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, says the Falklands is "a perennial sore spot in Argentine politics" and that since the 1980s, various governments have raised the issue in an attempt to rally support and to "stoke the fires of nationalism."

He thinks Milei's intervention is noteworthy given that he had previously been open to better relations with the UK on the issue. He agrees that it may be a strategy to "boost approval ratings at a time when the government is under a lot of strong domestic pressure."

Potentially transformative for the Falklands

Even if Milei sees political gain in the issue, the possibility of the Sea Lion project being successful would significantly raise the economic stakes for all concerned.

The project has a budget of $1.8 billion (€1.6 billion) and could generate revenues of more than double that for the Falkland Islands. The companies hope that at its peak, the field will produce up to 50,000 barrels per day and could last for up to 35 years.

That would substantially increase the Falklands' current annual GDP, which is almost entirely dependent on the volatile fishing sector and tourism. The administration is even looking into the possibility of creating a sovereign wealth fund if the oil project is successful.

"It's a very significant project for us with a lot of potential for our future," said Bragger. "It's been a big effort to get to this point and assuming all goes to plan, we want to retain as much value as possible."

However, beyond playing to domestic politics, Milei may also spy an opportunity for Argentina to position itself as an energy player amid the war in Iran and the troubles in the Strait of Hormuz.

Argentina's own domestic oil sector is growing, with production surging at Patagonia's Vaca Muerta, one of the world's largest shale developments. Were his legal efforts to prove successful, there may be further gains.

"When natural resources overlay existing territorial disputes and bad blood, that tends to galvanize a lot of conflict," said Ziemer.

However, Bragger counters that Milei and Argentina have no legitimate claim to either the Falklands or whatever oil wealth may be extracted over the coming years.

"They don't respect our right to self-determination," he added. "They don't respect our right to develop our own resources. They just want to colonize us."

More economic pressure from Argentina

Milei plans to put pressure on the Falklands by stepping up existing economic sanctions. Andrea Clausen, chief executive of the Falklands since 2025, recently described this campaign as "economic warfare."

Many international suppliers and shipping companies already refuse to supply the Falklands for fear of angering Argentina. Now, Milei's government has initiated sanctions against 60 people involved in the Sea Lion project.

In a televised address last month, he also vowed to sanction the companies involved in the project. Such a move could cast doubt on the project, which previously collapsed in 2014 and 2020, due to financing troubles, oil-price weakness and delays caused by sanctions.

Navitas this week confirmed that two contractors had pulled out of the project due to sanctions concerns and that it was replacing them. There are also concerns that Milei could try to garner international support in favor of his position, with President Donald Trump recently suggesting that US support for the status quo on the islands was "under review."

Bragger plays this down, pointing to recent comments from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming support for the Falklands. Ziemer says it would be "very shocking" if the United States came down on the side of Argentina.

While uncertainty reigns over whether the oil project ultimately gets going or not, there is little expectation that the dispute could lead to a return of armed conflict like in 1982.

"That's a step too far, and the situation would have to dramatically deteriorate before we would see the potential for military conflict," said Ziemer.

Edited by: Tim Rooks

entries.title: Nobel Prize in literature goes to Canada's Anne Carson
entries.summary: Carson won for her "bold and inventive oeuvre." The decorated poet and essayist is known for her reverence for Latin and Greek classics.
entries.content:
LiteratureGlobal issues

Nobel Prize in Literature goes to Canada's Anne Carson

October 8, 2026

Carson won for her "bold and inventive oeuvre." The decorated poet and essayist is known for her reverence for Latin and Greek classics.

The Swedish Academy awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature to Anne Carson on Thursday, praising her "bold and inventive oeuvre."

Her work has "in playful dialogue with the classical tradition...created new forms for contemporary literature," said Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the academy.

The 76-year-old writer is a longtime professor of classics, creative writing, and comparative literature at prestigious institutions like McGill and Princeton universities. She is only the 19th woman of 123 laureates to win the award.

What is Anne Carson known for?

Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson moved with her family among several small towns in Canada during her youth. She has credited a beloved Latin teacher for sparking her interest in language and classics.

Her first book of criticism, 1986’s Eros the Bittersweet, was published to great acclaim and has had significant influence on other classicists, poets, and even film and television. Carson has also published her own poetry such as the 2001 collection The Beauty of the Husband as well as highly regard translation of ancient Greek poets such as Sappho and Sophocles.

Carson is also heavily influenced by the King James Bible and more modern writers including Emily Dickinson and Virginia Woolf. She has received numerous awards such as the T.S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur fellowship, and the PEN/Nabokov Award.

Deeply private, Carson often declines to speak about her personal life in interviews and discourages autobiographical interpretations of her work. However, she did revealed in 2024 that she has Parkinson's disease.

Who else has received a Nobel Prize so far?

  • The Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded Monday to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work on optogenetics, a method of controlling nerve cells with light, that makes it possible to study how the brain works.
  • The Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded Tuesday to Francis Halzen, a Belgian-born astrophysicist whose efforts helped demystify a rare group of neutrinos that launched a new era of astronomy.
  • The Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Henri B. Kagan of France and Kenso Soai of Japan on Wednesday, for solving the longstanding mystery of homochirality in living organisms.

What happens next?

The winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature receives prize money of 12 million Swedish kronor, equivalent to about $1.2 million. The winner also receives a medal and a diploma at an official ceremony in December, and is expected to deliver a speech known as a Nobel lecture.

On Friday, the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize will be announced, followed by the Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel on Monday.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: South Korea recalls Ukraine ambassador amid POW dispute
entries.summary: South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine. Seoul is upset about a transfer of North Korean prisoners of war being made public knowledge at the UN and had demanded — but not received — an apology.
entries.content:
Ukraine

South Korea recalls Ukraine ambassador amid POW dispute

October 8, 2026

South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine. Seoul is upset about a transfer of North Korean prisoners of war being made public knowledge at the UN and had demanded — but not received — an apology.

South Korea said on Thursday that it would recall its ambassador to Ukraine amid a deepening diplomatic rift over making the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul public last month. 

The two countries have been at loggerheads since Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's speech at the UN General Assembly, during which he spoke about the capture and later the transfer of two North Korean soldiers who had been fighting against Ukraine alongside Russian forces. 

South Korea has called for an apology from Ukraine, saying the comments breached a confidentiality agreement and could put the POWs' families still in North Korea at risk.

Kyiv, meanwhile, has said no such agreement existed and voiced a desire to smooth over a "diplomatic understanding," but stopped short of apologizing.

What did South Korea's Foreign Ministry say about recalling its ambassador?

"The govenment has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine," Seoul's Foreign Ministry said on Thursday.

"The government hopes that all outstanding issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and wil continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end," it said.

Last week, President Lee Jae Myung called for a "public apology" from Kyiv and said South Korea would take "additional measures" if one was not forthcoming. He said that during the prisoner swap, "the Ukrainian side demanded confidentiality and agreed to it, but unilaterally disclosed it."

When challenged with what Myung described as "utmost courtesy," he said Kyiv instead denied the existence of a confidentiality agreement, making him out to be a liar, and spoke of the prospect of war on the Korean peninsula.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, meanwhile, had spoken of a "diplomatic misunderstanding" that he said "we sincerely hope to resolve."

Bilateral tensions also emerged this week amid the publication of an investigative report in The Guardian claiming that fuel was being shipped to Russia from South Korea via sanctioned tankers, alleviating the strains on diesel supplies amid Ukraine targeting Russian refineries and other oil infrastructure.

South Korea has walked a fine line on Russia's war in Ukraine, providing humanitarian and non-lethal equipment to Kyiv, as well as financial assistance, but also seeking to maintain cordial ties with Russia, which has a small stretch of border with North Korea near Vladivostock.

North Korea, meanwhile, sent troops to help Russia reclaim the border region of Kursk that Ukraine was able to partially occupy, and has since celebrated this deployment at home with much fanfare, while seeking closer ties to Putin's Russia.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: As Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian data centers, could Ukraine soon be offline?
entries.summary: As Russia targets Ukraine's data centers more and more, experts say the country's internet system is too robust to shut down entirely. However, services could become more expensive.
entries.content:
October 8, 2026

As Russia targets Ukraine's data centers more and more, experts say the country's internet system is too robust to shut down entirely. However, services could become more expensive.

Hackers and power outages were once the largest threat to Ukraine's data centers. Now, it is the buildings themselves that are in the cross hairs.

Since early September, Russia has been  targeting these centers, which house the physical infrastructure needed to store digital information, systematically.

Digital infrastructure in and around the capital Kyiv was already affected but after the attacks, several television channels and streaming services were temporarily unavailable. Subscribers to several cable networks also reported that they had difficulties connecting.

Why is Russia targeting Ukrainian data centers?

The servers and computer systems needed to store data and keep online services operating smoothly are a crucial target because if they are damaged, it can have a nationwide effect. All online systems, ranging from news portals, state registries, banking and finance, need functioning data centers to operate smoothly.

Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha said Russia had targeted major Ukrainian data centers to disrupt the flow of information. "As Russia isn’t achieving its goals on the battlefield, it is seeking new ways to destabilize life in Ukraine and terrorize civilians."

Could Ukraine go offline?

Despite widespread damage caused by Russian attacks, experts do not believe the country risks having a complete internet blackout. Telecommunications expert Oleksandr Glushchenko told DW that this was because the entire sector was quite decentralized. 

"The industry was never regulated in Ukraine, and no multi-million licenses were required,” he explained. "Entering the market was very affordable, which is why thousands of businesses started offering their services."

He added that Ukrainians could choose between multiple providers — and in some cases up to 10. This competition, he said, meant that Ukraine had "some of the best internet provider services in the world."

At the same time, he noted, damage caused by kinetic attacks could cause certain providers to "go dark" while repairs took place.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian lawmaker Oleksandr Fediienko, who is a member of the parliamentary Committee on National Security, Defense and Intelligence, posted similar sentiments on the social network Facebook: "Will the internet disappear in Ukraine? Of course not. The infrastructure will be restructured, and alternative sites will be established." He added that the Russian attacks made no sense because Ukrainian providers were able to restore service so quickly.

Serhii Beskrestnov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's advisor on defense technology, said that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian data centers were part of a wider campaign. "They've already been scaring us with claims that there won't be food or fuel, and now they're scaring us with the prospect of losing internet access," he wrote on Facebook.

How can data and devices be protected?

Glushchenko said that even if a server was destroyed, its data would be available from other data centers where it was stored, including abroad. "The system can automatically switch to a different data center," he explained.

He pointed out that telecommunications companies also stored copies with cloud services offered by providers such as Google and Amazon.

Oleksandr Olshanskyi, the founder of the Ukrainian web hosting provider MiroHost and also the head of the leading Ukrainian IT service company Internet Invest, told the Ukrainian news agency RBC-Ukraine that his data center had been almost totally destroyed but that this had not made a major difference. He said that the vast majority of his clients remained unaffected, as they could fall back on operation capacities in Poland and the Czech Republic. "I'm only left with about 150 out of 20,000 to 25,000 clients, who for some reason did not shift, duplicate or secure their data," he explained.

Tech experts have recommended that Ukrainian data centers place a higher priority on decentralization, saying they should be as spread out as possible geographically, and also that data should be cloned and secured in other data centers abroad. Moving infrastructure into underground spaces could also be a solution, but this would translate into extra costs for customers.

"We've grown accustomed to having the fastest and cheapest internet in Europe, and the best technical support," Fediienko said but pointed out that this was "about to change."

Beskrestnov also expected the price of internet services to rise soon, to cover the costs of repairing damage to infrastructure.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

entries.title: Ukraine says 30 killed, 18 wounded in Russian attack on passenger buses in Kramatorsk
entries.summary: Authorities in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk have suspended public transport following the deadly attack near the front line.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Russian strike on buses in Ukraine's Kramatorsk kills 30

October 8, 2026

Authorities in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk have suspended public transport following the deadly attack near the front line.

A Russian glide bomb strike on two passenger buses in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 30 people and wounded 18 others, authorities said on Thursday.

The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office confirmed the death toll following the attack on Telegram on Thursday morning.

What do we know about the attack?

The bomb struck the buses as they travelled along a street, also hitting a residential building, according to Ukrainian authorities.

The regional governor's office reported the same figures and said public transport services had been suspended.

Images released by prosecutors showed a burned-out bus and bodies lying on the ground.

The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office said it had opened a preliminary investigation into a suspected war crime.

Governor Vadym Filashkin said Russian forces were deliberately targeting civilian transport.

"For them, a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one strike can kill as many people as possible," he said.

"Russia deliberately disregards all conceivable rules of warfare and the norms of international humanitarian law," he said. "It chooses targets where it can cause the most pain to civilians."

"Under such circumstances, we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers," he said. "The safety of the residents of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk is now above all else."

The attack came a day after Russian strikes killed 30 people across Ukraine, including 22 in a residential building in the northern city of Pryluky.

Separate Russian strikes on Kyiv on Thursday killed three people and wounded 13 others, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko.

Why is Kramatorsk strategically important?

Kramatorsk lies close to the front line in Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region. It is one of the main Ukrainian-held cities in the Donetsk region, which Russia claims to have annexed.

The city has served as a key military logistics hub throughout much of the war and forms part of Ukraine's heavily defended eastern "fortress belt."

Russian forces have advanced toward the city's eastern outskirts, prompting calls for remaining civilians to evacuate to safer areas.

Ukrainian forces have been conducting counterattacks in the surrounding area in recent weeks, claiming to have recaptured several square kilometers of territory.

Kramatorsk was briefly occupied by pro-Russian separatists in 2014 before Ukrainian forces retook it.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: UK scales back Jerusalem consulate after Israel dispute
entries.summary: Britain says its diplomatic mission will remain open with reduced staff, despite Israel's order to close the nearly 200-year-old consulate.
entries.content:
Palestinian Territories

UK scales back Jerusalem consulate after Israel dispute

October 8, 2026

Britain says its diplomatic mission will remain open with reduced staff, despite Israel's order to close the nearly 200-year-old consulate.

Britain has withdrawn diplomats from its consulate in East Jerusalem after reaching an agreement with Israel over the future of the diplomatic mission.

According to Israel, the consulate had ceased operating in its previous capacity. Britain insisted that the building would remain open under the name UK Mission, Jerusalem.

The move follows a diplomatic dispute over British measures targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

What has happened to the British consulate?

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said 20 British diplomats, including the consul general, were ending their assignments and leaving Israel.

Seven diplomats would be allowed to continue working from the building, although their activities would be "very limited," he said.

The consulate's diplomatic emblem and sign were removed from the building on Thursday.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said London had temporarily withdrawn some staff and their families to ensure their safety.

He insisted the mission would remain independent and operational, continuing to provide "vital services" and work with Palestinians.

Miliband said Britain did not accept that Israel had the legal right to close the consulate, which was established in 1838.

Why did Israel order the consulate to close?

Israel ordered the closure on September 8 in retaliation for British measures against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Britain joined other countries in announcing trade restrictions and sanctions targeting settlements and individuals linked to settler violence against Palestinians.

Israel condemned the measures as a diplomatic attack.

The British consulate has traditionally handled relations with Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, separately from Britain's embassy in Tel Aviv.

Israel captured East Jerusalem in 1967 and subsequently annexed it, a move not recognized by most countries, including Britain.

Miliband said Britain would not take retaliatory diplomatic action while talks with Israel continued.

He reaffirmed London's support for a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher
